gov_personnel.name: Zach Barber, Dennis Higgs, Derek Hostetler

data.leadership_messages: 1. The contractor has built a theoretically sound planning structure and agile workflow for software, but the WBS and supporting documents currently do not contain sufficient information to understand scope of Control Accounts/System Features
data.rationale: WBS Descriptions do not provide enough information to understand the scope of work contained within SW WBS Control Accounts. With the switch to Feature Based accounts, we need to be provided artifacts containing descriptions of what software capability is captured in the System Features/Control Accounts. A description stating, ”CS SW Pad Launch Flight Enablers, using a framework of Incremental Features. This includes Incremental Feature definition, software requirements, software design, software implementation and unit tests, unit integration and testing, and Incremental Feature integration, following the development logic outlined in the Software Development Plan (SDP)." does to not adequately explain the scope of software work. Understanding that this Control Account means software initializing for Wing Ops and Launch Execution subsystems requires either the list of associated Incremental Features and/or investigation of NG’s Jira projects. Neither of those have been provided.

areas.text: Artifacts do not provide enough information to understand the scope of work contained within Software WBS Control Accounts. The transition to Feature-Based Control Accounts has created a critical information gap: current WBS descriptions are insufficiently detailed, and the contractor's reliance on rolling-wave planning means that future Incremental Features (Work Packages) are not defined upfront to establish a baseline. While near-term scope is detailed inside Jira, program leadership must have high-level scope clarity directly within the baseline planning artifacts rather than being forced to search through execution-level software tools.While a product-oriented, feature-based structure is conceptually appropriate for agile software, the decomposition stops at too high a level for the baseline.To establish confidence in the PMB, the contractor must provide artifacts containing detailed descriptions of the specific software capabilities captured within each System Feature and Control Account. This level of understanding requires either:1. A predefined list of associated Incremental Features / Work Packages, or2. Significantly enhanced, highly detailed descriptions of the Control Accounts within the CWBS Dictionary.The contractor’s proposed rolling-wave planning approach dictates that they “will decompose the Incremental Features from the Planning Packages prior to the start of the next PI and after Incremental Feature lockdown agreement across Command Systems.” While rolling-wave planning is standard practice in Agile development, performing decomposition of Incremental Features until right before execution prevents the Government from establishing an upfront baseline. The Government cannot verify, measure, or have confidence in the scope of a Control Account when the underlying Work Packages are entirely undefined.For the current and immediately upcoming Program Increments (PIs), the contractor does provide detailed decomposition; however, this data exists solely within their internal Jira instance.While Jira is the correct tool for day-to-day engineering execution, it is not a substitute for formal program management artifacts. Government Program Managers and Analysts should not be required to dig through active developer backlogs and software management tools to piece together a basic understanding of a Control Account’s contractual scope. This information must be maintained and easily accessible within the contract baseline documentation.

While the contractor has established a conceptually sound planning hierarchy and logical workflows, this framework remains largely unpopulated. The foundational ambiguity regarding Control Account scope (identified in Assessment Area 1) fundamentally prevents the contractor from translating their theoretical planning structure into an executable, resource-loaded Integrated Master Schedule (IMS).The contractor has successfully demonstrated a mature theoretical approach to schedule planning. The designated workflow effectively maps how software capabilities will transition through the engineering lifecycle, moving systematically from Feature Definition into Systems Engineering, through Software Development, and culminating in Integration & Test. Furthermore, the methodology for breaking these phases down into Incremental Features and Work Packages within their Jira and QBD constructs is logical and repeatable.Despite possessing a viable planning architecture, the contractor lacks the foundational data required to execute it. Schedule development cannot occur in a vacuum; it is fundamentally dependent on a clear understanding of the scope. Because the contractor cannot currently articulate the specific scope boundaries of each Control Account, they are subsequently unable to populate their planning hierarchy with actual tasks, durations, or resource requirements.In its current state, the contractor has built a robust schedule planning engine but has not provided the fuel (scope and task data) required to run it. Until the underlying scope is clearly defined and the associated data is entered into the planning constructs, the contractor is not ready for credible IMS loading or Performance Measurement Baseline (PMB) implementation.

The contractor has demonstrated a baseline understanding of software integration requirements at a conceptual level. The proposed planning packages do include structural placeholders for integration and testing tasks. This indicates that their core planning methodology recognizes the need for these activities, establishing a theoretical foundation for future cross-product coordination. While the contractor’s theoretical process for incorporating integration and testing tasks into planning packages is conceptually sound, the actual data is absent from the Work Breakdown Structure (WBS). Similar to findings in Assessment Areas 1 and 2, the theoretical framework has not been populated with actual data. Because the specific integration and testing tasks are not yet defined or present within the WBS architecture, the Government cannot evaluate the realism of the integration approach.Furthermore, observed breakout sessions reveal some organizational siloing between the Hardware and Software teams. The current inability or unwillingness of cross-functional teams to discuss Hardware/Software (HW/SW) integration due to differing methodologies presents a risk to overall program execution and IMS maturity.

Strength 1: P – 4 The contractor has established a logical and repeatable theoretical planning hierarchy to manage software development. The defined workflow progression (moving systematically from Feature Definition

Integration & Test) within their Jira and QBD constructs demonstrates a mature understanding of agile execution. This framework provides confidence that, once underlying scope data is populated, the fundamental execution logic and sequencing will be sound.
Strength 2: S – 5 The contractor’s utilization of Jira to manage active Program Increment (PI) workflows demonstrates a strong alignment with agile value streams at the execution level. While not currently integrated into the formal baseline artifacts, the existing Jira configuration provides a practical and effective mechanism for tracking near-term, day-to-day software development tasks and handoffs within the current PI.
Strength 3: I – 1 The contractor’s proposed planning packages include structural placeholders for integration and testing tasks. This demonstrates an upfront acknowledgment that integration activities must eventually be accounted for in the planning architecture, establishing a necessary structural foundation for future cross-product scheduling.
data.concerns: Concern 1: S – 3 CWBS Dictionary descriptions for Software Control Accounts are insufficiently detailed, providing only nominal information about the capabilities captured within System Features. Because the contractor relies on rolling-wave planning to decompose Incremental Features just prior to a PI, the baseline artifacts lack immediate scope definition. Risk: The Government cannot verify if all contractual requirements are assigned or understand Control Account boundaries, creating a high risk of deferred scope, overlapping efforts, and an inability to establish a credible Performance Measurement Baseline (PMB).Concern 2: P – 2 (Planning Structure and Task Definition Maturity)The proposed Feature-Based Control Account is excessively broad in scope, spanning across multiple Integrated Product Teams (IPTs) rather than being bounded by logical organizational lines. Due to this oversized design, progress and performance will be difficult to accurately measure or track at the Control Account level. To assess true program status, the Government will likely need to track completion and earned value at the lower Work Package/Incremental Feature level. However, because the contractor's rolling-wave planning process defers the decomposition of these Work Packages until immediately prior to each Program Increment (PI), this critical execution-level data does not yet exist. Risk: Without defined Work Packages or distinct Control Account boundaries, the Government has no mechanism to measure actual progress or evaluate schedule health. This structure will likely mask development bottlenecks, drive severe tracking difficulties, and render early Earned Value Management (EVM) and IMS-loading efforts highly inaccurate.Concern 3: I – 4 Breakout sessions reveal organizational siloing and a lack of cross-functional coordination between Hardware and Software teams. Hardware teams actively avoid discussing software dependencies, leaving HW/SW interfaces undefined. Risk: Without joint planning and a shared understanding of inter-product handoffs, there is a high probability of interface failures, integration bottlenecks, and schedule delays during physical system integration
data.questions: Follow-up 1: S – 1 Information Gap: The Government lacks visibility into the total planned software scope prior to PI execution. Action Needed: Request the contractor provide a preliminary software roadmap, capability matrix, or enhanced CWBS Dictionary that explicitly maps specific software functionalities to the proposed Feature-Based Control Accounts to establish a baseline understanding of scope prior to detailed PI decomposition.Follow-up 2: I – 1 Unresolved Assumption: It is unclear how agile software delivery will synchronize with hardware schedules. Action Needed: Require the contractor to present a HW/SW Integration Strategy. The contractor must demonstrate exactly how agile software milestones will map to, constrain, or enable traditional hardware integration events.Follow-up 3: P – 2 (Planning Structure and Task Definition Maturity)Information Gap: The organizational boundaries and tracking mechanisms for cross-IPT Control Accounts are undefined.Action Needed: Request the contractor deliver a Control Account / IPT Mapping Matrix and a process demonstration showing how they intend to isolate, track, and report progress for work within a single Control Account that is actively being executed by multiple distinct engineering teams.
data.integration: Observation 1: Hardware/Software Integration & PI AlignmentThere is a critical scheduling and data dependency between the Agile software development cadence and traditional hardware integration milestones. Software releases are planned via Program Increments (PIs), but Hardware nodes require specific software baselines at fixed dates to conduct physical integration and checkout. Not clear where the mapped alignment between the exists.Observation 2: Shared Test Environments (System Integration Lab - SIL)The software development teams are dependent on physical or virtual test environments (e.g., SILs or digital twins) provided by the Hardware and Infrastructure teams. Software cannot complete its defined Integration & Test phase without access to these shared resources. Coordination is required to ensure that the hardware team prioritizes the build-out and availability of the SIL environments to match the software team's PI testing schedule.
